title: The Proverbs of Solomon Begin: Two Ways in Two Lines
summary: A new heading, “The proverbs of Solomon”, opens the book's largest collection. The long poems of chapters 1 to 9 give way to short, self-contained sayings, most of them two lines that set the righteous against the wicked and the wise against the fool. This first chapter gathers sayings on work and harvest, on wealth gained honestly or dishonestly, and above all on speech: lips, mouth, and tongue that either give life or conceal violence.
story: Chapters 1 to 9 were a father's extended appeal to his son, with Wisdom and Folly calling out like two hostesses inviting the young man into their houses. That appeal has been made. Now the book hands the son the contents of Wisdom's house: hundreds of compact sayings to be learned, memorized, and turned over in real situations. The first verse picks up right where the prologue left off, with a wise son and a foolish one, so the reader knows these sayings are still the family instruction of chapters 1 to 9 in a new form. From here to 22:16 the book mostly moves in small units rather than a single argument, and the reader's task changes from following a speech to pondering one saying at a time.
historical:
The heading credits this collection to Solomon, king of Israel in the tenth century BC, whom 1 Kings 4 remembers as a man of wide wisdom who spoke thousands of proverbs. Many readers take the heading at face value; others think it marks the collection as belonging to the Solomonic tradition of royal wisdom, gathered and extended by later scribes, and Proverbs 25:1 shows that the court of King Hezekiah (around 715 to 686 BC) was still copying Solomon's sayings centuries later. A curious detail supports the heading's importance to the editors: the consonants of Solomon's name in Hebrew add up to 375, and the collection that runs from 10:1 to 22:16 contains exactly 375 verses. Some scholars think this is deliberate, a kind of signature, though it proves nothing about who first spoke any given line.

The world behind these sayings is mostly the ordinary life of Israel's villages and towns rather than the palace: fathers and mothers, fields and harvests, neighbors, lenders, rumor, and reputation. Wise sayings of this kind were common across the ancient Near East, and Egypt and Mesopotamia both produced collections of instructions for young men. Israel's collection shares the form but roots it in the LORD, who appears four times in this chapter alone.
cultural:
Verse 5 assumes an agricultural year that every first reader lived by. Grain was harvested in late spring and early summer, and fruit through the summer, and a family's survival through the winter rains depended on getting it in on time. A son who slept through harvest did not simply miss a chore; he endangered the household, and so he is called a disgraceful son, one who brings shame on the family's name. Honor and shame were public currencies, which is why verse 7 can say that the name of the wicked will rot: a person lived on in the memory of the community, and to be forgotten or remembered with disgust was a kind of second death.

The household itself was the first school. Verse 1 names both father and mother, and the grief of a foolish son falls on both. Instruction happened at meals, in the fields, and at the city gate, and it happened by word of mouth. That helps explain the chapter's heavy attention to lips and tongue. In a culture with few written records, a person's word was contract, testimony, and reputation all at once.
literary: Almost every verse here is antithetical parallelism: two lines joined by but, the second saying the same truth from the opposite side. The righteous (tsaddiq) and the wicked (rasha) appear more often than any other pair. The chapter is not random, though it is not an essay either. Sayings are linked by catchwords and repeated lines. Verse 6 and verse 11 end with the identical line, “the mouth of the wicked conceals violence”, and verses 8 and 10 end with “foolish lips will come to ruin”. Verses 18 to 21 and 31 to 32 form clusters on speech. Verses 27 to 30 gather sayings on the long-term security of the righteous. Reading well means slowing down: each saying is a small poem meant to be memorized and chewed, and its meaning often comes from setting it beside its neighbor.

outline.t: Wealth, hunger, and work at harvest
Blessing and the mouth of the wicked
Love, correction, and the power of speech
The LORD's blessing, desire, and the slacker
The lasting security of the righteous and their speech

doctrines.note: Wisdom in Proverbs is skill at living in God's world. This chapter shows it is not merely cleverness: the wise are also the righteous, and wisdom shows up in diligence, restraint of the tongue, and teachability (verses 8, 17, 19).

The LORD is behind the order the sayings describe. He does not let the righteous go hungry (verse 3), his blessing enriches (verse 22), and his way is a refuge (verse 29). These are statements about how God has made the world to work, not a timetable for any one life.

Sin here is concrete and social: ill-gotten treasure, concealed violence, slander, winking to deceive, words multiplied carelessly. Verse 19 observes that where words are many, sin is unavoidable, a sober comment on how often wrongdoing travels by mouth.

words.note: Mashal, proverb. The word covers a wider range than the English proverb: a saying, a comparison, a parable, even a taunt song (Isaiah 14:4). At its root is the idea of likeness or comparison. A mashal sets two things side by side so the reader sees one in light of the other, which is exactly what the two-line sayings of this chapter do.

Tsaddiq, righteous, appearing thirteen times in this chapter. In the Old Testament the righteous person is not sinless but in right relation: faithful to God and fulfilling obligations to neighbor, family, and community. In Proverbs the righteous and the wise are nearly the same person seen from two angles, one moral and one practical.

Kasah, to cover. The chapter uses the same verb in opposite directions. The mouth of the wicked covers, that is, conceals, violence (verses 6 and 11), and the one who conceals hatred has lying lips (verse 18). But love covers all transgressions (verse 12), not by hiding wrong from justice but by refusing to keep stirring it up. The New Testament echoes verse 12 in James 5:20 and 1 Peter 4:8.

christ: Jesus stands in the line of Israel's wisdom teachers and surpasses it. He told his hearers that something greater than Solomon was among them (Matthew 12:42), and he taught in short, memorable sayings and in parables, the same family of forms as the mashal. His story of two builders, one wise and one foolish (Matthew 7:24-27), is this chapter's contrast between the righteous who are secure forever and the wicked swept away by the whirlwind (verse 25), now made to turn on hearing and doing his words. Paul goes further and calls Christ the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). The link to this chapter is not prediction; Proverbs 10 does not speak of a Messiah. It is that the way of wisdom the sayings describe takes on a human face in him, and the love that covers transgressions (verse 12) is finally what he does at the cross.

hard.q: Are these sayings promises? Don't the righteous sometimes go hungry and die young?
hard.a:
Read as guarantees, verses like 3, 27, and 30 are simply false, and the Bible knows it. Job is a righteous man who loses everything; Ecclesiastes observes that the race is not always to the swift and that the righteous sometimes perish in their righteousness; many psalms cry out because the wicked prosper. The answer is in the genre. A proverb describes how life usually goes in a world God has ordered: diligence tends toward plenty, dishonesty tends toward ruin, a reputation for integrity tends to last. It is a true generalization, not a contract with a date attached. Proverbs itself signals this when it later places two opposite sayings side by side (26:4-5) and leaves the reader to judge which one fits the moment.

Some interpreters add that many of these sayings look past the immediate to the final outcome, since the righteous are secure forever (verse 25) in a way that death does not cancel. Others stress that Proverbs speaks mainly of this life and deliberately leaves the exceptions to Job and Ecclesiastes. Either way, the sayings are wisdom to live by, not formulas to hold God to.

questions: Verse 12 says love covers all transgressions. What is the difference between covering an offense in love and concealing it in a way that protects wrongdoing?
Many of these sayings are about speech. Which one describes your own tongue most accurately, for good or ill?
How does reading a proverb as a description of how life usually goes, rather than as a guarantee, change the way you read verses 3 and 27?
